texts.https://www.wired.com/story/over-a-third:
As generational cohorts go, Gen Z has been saddled with its share of labels. They scarcely have sex , are “ quiet quitters ” when it comes to office jobs, and, as they avoid traditional partnership, have learned to solomaxx .
Whether these labels are deserved or completely off the mark, what continually connects this unique class of young people is a desire to reconstruct how they think about connection.
In “ Friendship in an Online-Offline World: Digital Life, Connection and Wellbeing ” researchers from public polling firm Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children’s Hospital found that more than one-third of Gen Z (33 percent) rely on AI for companionship. The percentage was higher among daily AI users, spiking to 50 percent, and 42 percent among those with online-only friends.
Rather than measure the consequences of screen time alone, the report examines who Gen Z connects with and how those relationships not only account for their social lives but also how they impact their mental health. While in-person friendships were rated the highest for “strength and support” and were “associated with the most positive emotional experiences,” young people who rely on online-only friends or AI as a social companion may have higher odds of loneliness than those who do not.
Researchers examined three modes of what they consider close connection: in-person friendships, friendships that started IRL but are sustained online, and online-only friendships where a young person has never met their friend in real life. The survey, conducted between May and August, sampled 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries, and suggests that Gen Z benefits more from IRL relationships compared to digital ones, despite nearly half of young people in the US having at least one close online-only friend.
“Adolescence is a time when you thrive when you socialize, and so they’re looking for all of these contexts to socialize in,” says David Bickham, research director of the Digital Wellness Lab. “I don’t necessarily see it as, oh, these kids have some sort of major deficit and are looking to AI. I see it as these are young people who are growing up in a time of AI, the most powerful way to find information online, and the more they use it, they see and are more engaged with the social side of it.”
While AI may help fill a genuine social gap, it hasn’t yet taken the place of their IRL bonds. “In-person and digitally mediated friendships coexist within the same social life,” write the authors of the report.
When it comes to maintaining those affiliations, Instagram and Discord—surprisingly, not TikTok—were the top platforms in the US for staying in touch with online-only friends. Bickham also noted that “loneliness specifically may be something that these online relationships can’t quite compensate for.”
“Kids who are reporting loneliness really do things online that are consistent with trying to make friends. They talk to people they don't know, which is always a risk, but it’s also how you make friends,” Bickham says. The report found that Gen Z men, who were more likely to have digital friendships than women, often encountered new acquaintances through gaming, while young women mentioned social media as their most common category to cultivate connection. “What’s intriguing is that boys who are higher in social anxiety are less likely to make connections. They tend to do things by themselves, but when it comes to AI, what we found is that kids who are still lonely are going to seek out connections” with chatbots, Bickham says.
Recent debates over teen screen time have centered on whether digital devices are driving a youth mental health crisis or if the concerns are overstated. Some critics believe that by only measuring screen time it overlooks the type of content young people watch. This year, social media bans and age-restriction policies for minors took effect in Australia and the UK. In the US, where state legislators have introduced bills to curb addictive design features, a majority of Americans support banning kids under 16 from using social media, according to a recent Pew Research survey .
Jon-Patrick Allem, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health, wrote last year in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine that research on the topic has primarily focused on “blunt measures of screen time” and that doing so would “treat all content consumed online as uniform.” Allem concluded that this approach is “deficient” and called on researchers to set a new agenda that instead investigates the actual content kids were consuming, not just time spent.
It was also important to Bickham and his team to look beyond a surface-level analysis of screen time and consider the nature of the relationships being formed while young people were online, zeroing in on how that time is spent and who it’s spent with.
“It’s very difficult to measure screen time accurately in a survey. Mainly because half the kids told us this was something they’re doing all the time. A more important finding is the quality of relationship. It’s how you use these platforms that’s going to dictate your outcome, not just how long you use them for.”
A previous report from the Digital Wellness Lab mapped the use of AI among teenagers in the US, Brazil, and France and found that teens aged 13 to 17 were turning to AI for personal advice and creative work, in addition to companionship.
While researchers are wary of classifying the report as a permanent shift in how young people form relationships, they say it does signal a growing reliance on AI companionship as part of a pattern of digital social engagement unfolding among Gen Z.
“It wouldn’t be surprising if AI companionship becomes more common over the next five years as AI becomes integrated into young people’s everyday lives,” says Andrew Dugan, a principal researcher at Gallup. “But whether young people are turning to AI because they feel lonely, or whether AI companionship might reinforce those feelings, remains an important question for future research.”

The president says Beijing seeks to provide a ‘stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises’.
China’s President Xi Jinping has urged support for “free and open trade”, pitching Beijing as a stable partner – as opposed to President Donald Trump-led Washington – and pledging to stand up to trade protectionism.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Wednesday in Shenzhen, southern China, Xi took aim at rising “unilateralism and protectionism”.
His remarks appeared to be a veiled criticism of Trump’s America First policies, under which the United States has imposed tariffs on both allies and economic rivals.
Xi is due to meet Trump, who is travelling from the Philippines for the APEC leaders’ summit later on Wednesday. Xi and Trump are then due to hold an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On the sidelines of the APEC summit, Xi told business executives that the Asia Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth to remain stable and dynamic.
Trump’s America First approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone.
Washington also limits Chinese access to leading-edge US technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help power artificial intelligence (AI).
“We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains,” Xi said.
He added that China sought to “provide a more stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises” and would continue to expand access in its manufacturing and services sectors.
“Starting by lowering tariffs, expanding access, and exploring regulations and management standards, China will conduct deep-seated reform,” Xi said.
“While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said. “It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told the Associated Press news agency that Xi’s speech highlighted China’s aim to lead global industrial transformation.
“While he didn’t say so explicitly, his message was clear: China wants to be seen as a partner in global technology development, in contrast to Washington’s more restrictive approach,” Chen said, noting that Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia, or the US directly.
Xi’s message is “likely to resonate with many Global South countries, and reinforces Beijing’s effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington”, Chen added.

Republican incumbent beaten in race dominated by controversy over second candidate named Dan Sullivan
Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.
Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.
“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said in a statement on Tuesday.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she said. “As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families.”
Alaska was the last Senate race remaining to be called, and with Peltola’s victory, Democrats will control 56 seats in the upper chamber, after winning campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi. The party gained nine Senate seats in the midterms, a sweeping victory that will put them decisively back in the majority beginning next year, when they are expected to embark on an aggressive campaign of both lawmaking and investigating.
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, will join Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe, as the first two Native American women to serve in the US Senate.
Peltola faced significant controversy on the campaign trail, after the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in a scheme to recruit another Republican challenger, also named Dan Sullivan, to appear on the ballot.
Peltola’s campaign had denied any involvement in encouraging the second Sullivan’s run, and after state election officials tried to remove him, Alaska’s supreme court in June ruled he be allowed to appear on the ballot. Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted over the apparent ruse, and Alaska’s top federal prosecutor announced that criminal and civil inquiries were under way, while the state’s governor separately announced plans to open a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme.
Under Alaska’s voting system, the top four candidates from the nonpartisan primary advance to the November general election. Voters then rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives more than 50% on the initial round of counting, the last-place finisher is eliminated and that candidate’s supporters will have their second-choice votes counted.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had secured 50.1% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, while the incumbent senator received 45.8%. The other Sullivan had received just 1.7% while a third Republican, Gerald Heikes, received 2.1%.
Though Alaska is a Republican stronghold in presidential years, Peltola was viewed as a uniquely potent challenger to Sullivan, a two-term senator first elected in 2014 after defeating a Democrat.
A former state legislator who grew up in small communities along the Kuskokwim River in Alaska’s interior, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022, when she won a special election to replace the longtime Republican at-large congressman Don Young following his sudden death, and became the first Alaska native elected to Congress.
Peltola won a full term later that year, but lost re-election to Republican Nick Begich in 2024
In the race against Sullivan, Peltola’s fortunes appeared to rise as Alaskans grew frustrated with the price increases brought on by Trump’s tariffs and his decision to attack Iran earlier this year.
The state is the largest in the union, and dotted with cities and villages that are disconnected from the road system, and thus particularly hard-hit by the increases in oil prices the war caused. Gas prices in some interior Alaska communities jumped into the double-digits per gallon, while the rise in the price of diesel affected everything from groceries to alcohol, since many communities rely on shipments by sea.
Alaska is nonetheless a right-leaning state heavily reliant on its fishing and oil and gas industries. On the campaign trail, Peltola adopted the slogan “ fish, family, freedom ” to highlight how she would stand up for the state’s unique interests in Washington DC.
She has cast herself as an advocate for expanding oil production in the state, and addressing the issue of bycatch, or the accidental fishing of unwanted species, which some Alaskans believe is to blame for declining salmon runs.
Late in her campaign, Peltola posted a photograph of herself on Instagram from 1995, wearing the winner’s sash from the Miss National Congress of American Indians pageant. “Then and now, Alaska is at the heart of who I am,” she wrote.
Sullivan, meanwhile, stuck to Trump’s side, even as the president’s popularity declined nationwide, and especially in Alaska, according to some surveys. He did not join other vulnerable Republicans in urging an end to the war with Iran, while accusing Peltola of disrespecting voters after a report emerged that she had used a hompohobic slur and abused her staff.

Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in the race for Alaska’s Senate seat, delivering a final blow to Republicans in a midterm election rout following a race that drew accusations of cheating.
The Associated Press (AP) news agency called the race on Tuesday night, capping a contest that attracted national attention after an investigation alleged that aides to Peltola recruited another man named Dan Sullivan to run for office to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.
Peltola has denied any knowledge of the alleged decoy candidate plot.
Sullivan had pledged to accept the election outcome days after the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results if the Republican incumbent lost.
Peltola, in a statement on social media, said there “is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs and put Alaska first. Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”
Alaska also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, after former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by US President Donald Trump. AP has not yet called the US House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Representative Nick Begich.
The Alaska race is the last US Senate contest to be resolved in this year’s midterm elections, and Peltola’s victory expands the Democrats’ majority after they retook control of the chamber. The party already won campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and, most recently, Mississippi.
With Peltola’s victory, Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most since 1958. Republicans entered the midterms with a 53-47 majority, while Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin.
Peltola previously held the state’s lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026.
During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are often only accessible by air or water.
Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to distance herself from national Democrats and build a coalition around a platform of “Alaska first”.
“Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said. “I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.”
The race attracted a flood of spending by outside groups and at times turned negative, with the campaigns accusing each other of spreading lies. Trump and Vice President JD Vance made separate trips to the state in the month before the election in support of the incumbent.

Peltola, the first Alaska Native in the US Senate, ran a campaign that drew universal issues from her own Indigenous politics
Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton Hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska , to greet her supporters.
It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senate candidate from expressing her elation , bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.
Before she could speak, a volunteer shouted out from the back of the hall: “ Aarigaa! ” Peltola picked up the refrain, and threw it right back:
It was just one word. But it encapsulated something special about Peltola and her insurgent’s campaign to unseat the incumbent Republican US senator, Dan Sullivan.
“Aarigaa” is an Iñupiaq word that is commonly understood across Alaska’s 229 federally recognised tribes. It is a word of celebration, of relief almost, that roughly translates to: “Way to go!” or “Attaboy!”
Now, Peltola genuinely has a reason for exclaiming it. On Tuesday – two weeks after the midterm elections – the tortuous count was finally completed, and she was declared winner.
In prevailing, she becomes the first Alaska Native to take a seat in the US Senate .
“I was so happy at that moment,” said Ana Hoffman, a lifelong friend of the senator-elect’s who was present in the Sheraton ballroom. “ Aarigaa! It demonstrated through language what her campaign is all about: inclusion, representation, identity.”
The last US Senate race of the 2026 cycle to be called, Peltola’s victory carries with it several layers of significance. For US politics as a whole, it awards Democrats comfortable control of the upper chamber of Congress, with 56 seats to Republicans’ 44.
For Native Americans across the union, it marks the first time that seven Native people will be serving simultaneously in Congress – representatives Josh Brecheen and Tom Cole from Oklahoma, Sharice Davids from Kansas, Sean McCann from Michigan and Claire Valdez from New York; and senators Peggy Flanagan from Minnesota and Peltola from Alaska.
And for Alaska Natives, there is their own resounding cause to roar aarigaa : since Congress was convened 237 years ago, there have been more than 20,000 seats filled in the US House and Senate.
Among them, only 29 have been occupied by Native Americans, and of those Peltola is the only Alaska Native to have served in Congress. She won Alaska’s only House of Representatives seat in 2022, losing it two years later to the Republican Nick Begich, and in January she will take her Senate seat as part of the new intake.
Hoffman, who is president of the Native Corporation in Peltola’s home town of Bethel in western Alaska, said that her friend’s victory would uplift a people “who have been marginalized and underrepresented throughout generations. ‘Alaska Native’ will no longer be a concept in the Senate, it will be a colleague.”
The gaping lack of representation of Alaska Natives is no small thing for Alaska or the US. Alaska is home to about 40% of all federally recognized tribes in the union, and the one in five voters who are Indigenous amount to the largest proportion of the electorate in any state.
“Alaska Natives have played pivotal roles in US history, around decisions on land, resources and development. Yet their centrality to US decision-making still takes many people by surprise,” said Sonja Castañeda Dower, a congressional fellow with the American Political Science Association who has studied the power of Alaskan tribes.
Peltola is a Yup’ik Alaskan from Bethel, a town of fewer than 7,000 people that acts as the hub of 56 villages scattered along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers. Her Yup’ik name is Akalleq, or “the one who rolled”. Her mother was from the nearby community of Kwethluk; her father, a German American, came to Alaska from Nebraska to work as a pilot.
As a young girl, Peltola began fishing the Kuskokwim river with her father from the age of six. “We’d pass each other on the river,” said Hoffman, who lives in Bethel and is also Yup’ik. “We had fish camps near one another along the same slough.”
Peltola put Alaska Native issues and sensibilities at the center of her election campaign. She made exceptional efforts to reach out to communities that have rarely been included in the political process, travelling by floatplanes, four-wheelers and snowmachines to far-flung parts of the last frontier – a state that is larger in landmass than California and Texas combined.
Peltola showed up in more than 50 communities, some with a population of fewer than 300 people.
Yup’ik symbolism was embedded in her campaign. At campaign stops, she wore mukluk boots and Indigenous kuspuk shirts. The campaign’s circular logo was modelled on the Yup’ik eye, a traditional sign that also alludes to the eyewear made from wood or walrus ivory worn by Yup’ik people as protection against the blinding glare of the arctic snow.
“Peltola leaned into her Yup’ik identity as a qualification for advancing policies that appealed to a broad base of Alaskan supporters,” said Elise Blasingame, a political scientist specialising in Native American representation at Emory University, and a citizen of the Osage Nation. She added: “Look at her campaign’s merchandise. Who else would market a baby onesie saying: ‘I teethe on dried salmon’?”
You might also ask, who else would put salmon at the heart of an electoral contest for national office? The official mantra of the campaign was “Fish, family, freedom” – a slogan that neatly captures the dual nature of Peltola’s message and can be read in equal measure as an appeal to Native tribal people and as a paean to Alaskan and American patriotism.
Fish embody that double-edged message. As Peltola explained in an interview in October, about 80% of the diet of Yup’ik people has traditionally been fish, of which about half is salmon. “Our generic word for fish is the generic word for food,” she said. “ Neqa .”
The devastating decline of the catch of chinook salmon, or king salmon, along the Kuskokwim river in recent years, partly as a result of the climate crisis and partly through over-trawling in international waters in the Bering Sea, is an existential challenge for Alaska Native tribes. Their villages are sited on riverbanks along the salmon run.
“Fish, and our access to them, are the reason our communities exist,” Hoffman said.
But fish are also central to the entire economy of Alaska, Indigenous or not. The state accounts for about 60% of all wild seafood harvested across the US, and the combination of subsistence fishing, industrial fish processing and tourism is critical to Alaska’s 740,000 residents as a whole.
So when Peltola made a central pitch of her campaign that her rival, the incumbent Republican senator, was selling out the people in favor of big trawler companies, it spoke not just to the 20% of the electorate who are Alaska Native, but to all Alaskans. Without that, she would never have stood a chance – she had to reach the independent and wavering Republican voters who overwhelmingly elected Donald Trump in 2024 and for whom Native issues are not top priority.
Peltola, like Democrats across the country, hammered the issue of affordability on the campaign trail. When a gallon of milk costs as much as $21 in the most isolated parts of the state, and grocery prices are sky-high as a result of Donald Trump’s war with Iran, that is a concern for all Alaskans.
For Hoffman, that is the key to Peltola’s agonisingly delayed victory – she drew out of her own Indigenous politics what was universal for every voter.
“That’s the beauty about Mary, that she understood the universality of who we are as Alaskans. So the focus on access to fish, for Alaskans, that is like the pursuit of happiness.”

A wonder strike from Justin Devenny earned Northern Ireland top spot in Nations League Group B2 and promotion to the top tier of the competition. The Stoke player fired home on the volley from the edge of the area to earn a 1-1 draw away to Hungary , who would have leapfrogged Michael O’Neill’s side in the group with victory.
Northern Ireland had fallen 1-0 behind after a 35th-minute goal from the striker Barnabas Varga, who slotted home when one-on-one with the goalkeeper Pierce Charles after a defensive mix-up. The goal ended Northern Ireland’s proud record of not having conceded in this campaign and also sent Hungary to the top of the group in the live standings.
But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for O’Neill’s young outfit, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland’s one-point advantage as group leaders. As time ticked down, Hungary pushed forward in increasing desperation – with Rajmund Toth firing over late on – but Northern Ireland dug in with the defensive resilience which has been the cornerstone of their campaign.
“It’s a great feeling for us,” said O’Neill, who had to watch the game from the stands as he served a touchline ban. “We set out when we came into this level of the competition to first of all try and stay and we knew to be in the top two positions would help us.
“We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028 [qualification] but to come away unbeaten, to finish top, and to give the performance we’ve given against some very good teams, it’s very encouraging.”
In Wales’s group, Norway snatched a quarter-final berth thanks to Erling Haaland’s 96th-minute penalty against Denmark . It was Haaland’s second and completed a remarkable comeback from 2-0 down as the Danes were pipped for second place in Group A4.
Denmark, who began the day in second place in the standings and needed to avoid defeat to reach the knockout phase, led 2-0 inside 14 minutes through Rasmus Højlund and Pierre-Emile Højbjerg.
But Haaland pulled one back before half-time and, after Martin Ødegaard’s 83rd-minute equaliser had set up a grandstand finish, the Manchester City striker scored from the spot in the sixth minute of added time after the video assistant referee had ruled Joachim Andersen had handled in the area.
The two nations finished level on nine points and although Denmark had a better goal difference, Norway progressed on their head-to-head record after also winning the reverse fixture 3-2.
“It’s one of the crazier football years,” Haaland told TV2. “It’s fun to be a part of finishing it off in style. Ståle [Solbakken, Norway’s coach] said ⁠it before the match: ‘Let’s just get a good finish now to a completely indescribable football year.’ It’s fun to be Norwegian.”
Norway’s latest success came ​on the back of their memorable World Cup run, when Haaland ‌and Ødegaard led the country to the ‌quarter-finals in their first appearance at the tournament for 28 years. “It’s completely fantastic and fun,” Haaland said. “I should have had a hat-trick today, ‌but I’m happy with two goals, so that’s totally fine.”
The Republic of Ireland beat 10-man Kosovo 3-0 at the Aviva Stadium to go ahead of the visitors in the standings for Group B3 to secure second place and a spot in the promotion playoffs. The win also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month’s qualifying draw for that competition.
Kreshnik Hajrizi’s first-half handball on the line earned the Kosovo defender a red card and allowed Troy Parrott to bury the resulting penalty. The Republic were awarded a second spot-kick early in the second period after a foul by the goalkeeper Arijanet Muric, with Parrott again scoring. Jack Moylan’s header from a Liam Kitching cross made it 3-0.
What had been a largely uneventful encounter took a dramatic twist in the 26th minute, the red card incident sparked by Moylan’s cross, glanced on by Liam Scales to Parrott. His effort – clearly goalbound – was cleared off the line by Hajrizi, who extended his arm like a goalkeeper, and was immediately sent off.

After going 500 minutes without conceding a goal, Northern Ireland could be forgiven for having to make adjustments to play from behind.
Having travelled to Budapest knowing a point against Hungary would be enough to top Nations League B2, Barnabas Varga's strike after 35 minutes for the hosts at the Puskas Arena altered the picture and, for the first time in the campaign, left Michael O'Neill's side having to chase a game.
Their response to the deficit - on the pitch, from the bench and high in the stands where their suspended manager was watching the game - displayed the best characteristics of a side who had not won at this level before this unbeaten campaign.
While the point from a 1-1 draw in Budapest will be long remembered for Justin Devenny's brilliant equaliser and the scenes of celebration that greeted promotion to the competition's top tier for the first time, it was beyond the highlights and headlines that O'Neill saw the emerging qualities of his side.
"We went behind tonight and it was difficult, you know? Big stadium, big atmosphere, but we came out and played well in the second half and got what we needed from the game," said the manager.
"Those are things that I'm very pleased that are in this squad at such a young age. The technical side of the game we'll always look to improve on, but in terms of the physical, the tactical and the mental side of a game, we're very far ahead of where I thought we would be at this time."
Northern Ireland draw with Hungary to seal Nations League promotion
Hungary enjoyed more than 70% possession in the first half, and they could have been further than a goal ahead with Liverpool star Dominik Szoboszlai striking the base of the post after only five minutes.
O'Neill made his first change at half-time, bringing on veteran striker Josh Magennis, while Kieran Morrison, Brodie Spencer and Paul Smyth all followed in the second half.
Magennis and Morrison made a real impact before the equaliser, but it was the belief shown by all involved that O'Neill felt was key to the turnaround.
"I felt in the first half from where I was seeing the game, we just looked a little bit leggy which is natural," added O'Neill.
"I just felt we needed that freshness at the right points in the game that helped us, but it was the belief that we could get back into the game, and the belief that we could see the game out.
"I think we showed a lot of attributes that are in this squad at this moment in time and certainly in the second half that was that was the case."
For all the plaudits earned by this team who conceded just one goal in six games while picking up 12 points, among the most impressive aspects of the campaign has been who they have had to do without.
Talismanic Liverpool defender Conor Bradley has not played for this side in over 12 months through injury.
Ali McCann is another who missed both 2026 Nations League windows, while influential defender Daniel Ballard featured only in the first game in Georgia before a hamstring injury.
Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill was forced to pull out of the November squad through injury at a time when he would perhaps have been the most natural replacement for Jamie Donley after the striker picked up a second booking against Ukraine last week and had to miss the finale through suspension.
Having taken over an ageing squad four years ago, O'Neill has rebuilt his playing panel with a group that feels as if it is getting deeper with each international window.
"The encouraging thing is we have players on the outside - we've Bradley to come back in, Ballard to come back in, Ali McCann, young Ceadach, Eoin Toal," added the former Stoke City and Blackburn Rovers boss.
"We have good competition for places now. We're going to need that competition, and some players are going to miss out, but we are building depth to the squad that will help us going forward."
Come the next Nations League, that will be all the way into the uncharted territory of the top tier.

Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest , several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.
“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.
Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.
Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil , with others in Indonesia and India.
The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

Nvidia, 2027 mali yılının üçüncü çeyreği olarak kabul ettiği 25 Ekim'de sona eren üç aylık dönemin finansal sonuçlarına ilişkin telekonferans düzenledi.
Şirketin Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı Harvey Jones, buradaki konuşmasında, Nvidia'nın son derece güçlü bir şirket olduğunu, finansal performansının da bunu açıkça ortaya koyduğunu söyledi.
Yönetim Kurulunun 12 Kasım'da şirketin davranış kuralları, standartları ve kurum kültürüyle bağdaşmayan kişisel davranışlarının ortaya çıkmasının ardından Jensen Huang'ın başkanlık, CEO'luk ve yönetim kurulu üyeliği görevlerinden kendi isteğiyle istifa ettiğini duyurduğunu anımsatan Jones, Huang'ın istifasının oy birliğiyle kabul edildiğini ve kendisini yeniden CEO olarak görevlendirme niyetinde olmadıklarını aktardı.
Jones, Huang'ın istifasına ilişkin koşullar ve devam eden soruşturma hakkında herhangi bir açıklama yapmayacaklarını ve bu konudaki soruları yanıtlamayacaklarını belirtti.
Yeni CEO'nun belirlenmesi sürecinde şirket içinden ve dışından adayların değerlendirileceğini aktaran Jones, gelişmiş çip teknolojileri ve ulusal güvenlik dinamiklerinin sektörde büyük değişimlere yol açtığını, yeni CEO'nun bu koşulları çok dikkatli şekilde yönetmesi gerekeceğini ifade etti.
Jones, kalıcı CEO'nun mümkün olan en kısa sürede göreve getirilmesini istediklerini ancak doğru adayı bulmadan atama sürecini aceleye getirmeyeceklerini kaydetti.
Nvidia'nın geçici CEO'su ve Finans Direktörü (CFO) Colette Kress de iş açısından bakıldığında şirkette her şeyin alışılageldiği şekilde sürdüğünü belirtti.
Şirketin müşterileri, tedarikçileri ve iş ortaklarıyla iletişim halinde olduklarını anlatan Kress, "Hepsi de bizi yüzde 100 destekliyor. Müşterilerimiz, iş görünümüne desteklerini ve bu süreçte bize yardımcı olma isteklerini dile getiriyor. Ayrıca, arz ve talep arasındaki boşlukları daraltmak için tedarikçilerimizle de yakın bir işbirliği içinde çalışıyorlar." diye konuştu.
Son dönemde ​​​​​​​Huang'ın aralarında Çin adına casusluk yaptığı öne sürülen bir kadınla yaşadığı dahil evlilik dışı ilişkileriyle ilgili haberlerle gündeme gelen Nvidia'nın finansal sonuçlarına ilişkin düzenlediği telekonferans, piyasalar ve yatırımcılar tarafından yakından takip edildi.
Nvidia Yönetim Kurulu, 8 Kasım'da Jensen Huang'ın yabancı istihbarat faaliyetinin hedefi olduğuna ilişkin haberlerin ardından bağımsız soruşturma başlatıldığını duyurmuştu.
Öte yandan The New York Times gazetesinde yayımlanan bir haberde, Huang'ın şirkette kendisine bağlı bir yöneticiyle de evlilik dışı ilişki yaşadığı iddia edilmişti.
Nvidia 12 Kasım'da ise Huang'ın başkanlık, üst yöneticilik ve yönetim kurulu üyeliği görevlerinden derhal geçerli olmak üzere ayrıldığını, şirketin başkan yardımcısı ve finans direktörü Colette Kress'in geçici CEO olarak atandığını bildirmişti.
Nvidia'dan ayrılmasının ardından dün ilk kez açıklama yapan Huang, Yönetim Kurulunun geri dönmesinin hissedarların, çalışanların, şirketin ve ABD'nin çıkarları için en iyisi olacağına karar vermesi halinde CEO olarak görevine dönmeye hazır olduğunu ifade etmişti.
Anadolu Ajansı web sitesinde, AA Haber Akış Sistemi (HAS) üzerinden abonelere sunulan haberler, özetlenerek yayımlanmaktadır. Abonelik için lütfen iletişime geçiniz.
Bu haberde bir hata mı var? Her türlü talep, şikâyet ve görüş için okur temsilcimize ulaşabilirsiniz.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4:
Higher petrol and diesel prices pushed the UK's inflation rate up again last month, official figures show.
Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
Elevated oil prices also affected the wider economy, the ONS said, continuing to drive up the cost of raw materials and goods leaving factories.
Inflation risks being pushed higher in the coming months. Gas and electricity bills are forecast to jump by 26% in January, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, adding £443 to annual household energy costs when a new price cap comes into force.
Prices have surged in recent months because of the US-Iran war, with the Bank of England raising interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.
Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rate rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.
Higher interest rates increase the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.
Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.
VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.
But with household annual energy costs forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".
Sophie, who manages a cafe at the Old Boat Corner community centre in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk".
"I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said.
"I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa."
Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs".
Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October.
Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins.
But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."
Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.
Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.
But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.
And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years.
Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates.
It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028.
In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested.
A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there".

Illegal activities in the Amazon pose grave risks to uncontacted Indigenous groups like Brazil’s Awa, advocates stress.
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups , mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

Iranian officials said the US military conducted airstrikes on Qeshm Island in southern Iran on Tuesday evening, with locals reporting at least five explosions.
Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of Hormozgan, told the official IRNA news agency that the US strikes did not caused damage to residential or commercial districts, adding that "the situation on Qeshm Island is under control and all relief, service and executive bodies are on full alert."
Iranian news agency IRNA reported that "the sound of five to six explosions was heard in the city of Qeshm," while the semi-official Fars news agency wrote quoting "residents of Qeshm Island" that the sound of several explosions were heard north-west of the city of Qeshm. with smoke billowing at the same time.
US officials confirmed late Tuesday that US fighter jets struck Iranian missile launch sites on the island, in the same pattern as over the previous days, in retaliation for Iran’s targeting of US personnel and assets.
The US airstrikes follow multiple incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, in which at least five ships hit naval mines while sailing through what Iran calls "unauthorised" routes in the waterway.
“Safe passage requires coordination with the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran, transit through designated safe zones, and having navigation systems switched on,” the Iranian army announced in a statement.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Tuesday that it shot down a US MQ-1 Predator reconnaissance and combat drone in the southern waters of Iran, near Qeshm Island. According to the Guard, this would be the eighteenth drone of this type that its forces have destroyed.
The IRGC said in a statement it used a "new advanced air defence system" which allegedly tracked and destroyed this drone at 13:45 local time.
Earlier on Tuesday, the IRGC claimed said it carried out a drone attack against a US radar system at Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa Airbase. Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, and US' Central Command (CENTCOM) said that they intercepted the drones, without any damage.
The IRGC said the attack was carried out in response to "repeated violations of Iran’s airspace by US military drones".
Since the start of the Iran war in February, Tehran has tried to restrict traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and has insisted that ships pass only along routes that the Islamic Republic has authorised.

Haiti announced on Tuesday that it formalised a "cooperation agreement" with El Salvador, the same day thousands of Haitians showed support in the streets of Port-au-Prince for soldiers sent by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs in the capital.
"The Council of Ministers has approved the Cooperation agreement between the Republic of Haiti and the Republic of El Salvador," according to a Facebook post from the Haitian executive, who called it "a new stage in strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation."
Signs carried by the demonstrators on Tuesday read "Thank you, Bukele," and "Long live Bukele," according to photographs taken by an AFP journalist.
"Bukele, the country belongs to you! Do whatever you want with it," some chanted in the streets of a capital long subsumed by gang violence that has seized control of large sections.
Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from his country went missing during an operation of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The new Salvadoran deployment, despite being separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought reinforcements.
"We are asking President Bukele to ignore the detractors and to continue supporting Haiti," a demonstrator who declined to be identified for security reasons told AFP.
Numerous armed forces are now operating in Haiti, with uncertain levels of coordination, including the Haitian police and army, the multinational GSF, foreign mercenaries and most recently, the Salvadoran soldiers.
Bukele, whose forceful gang crackdown at home has won public support but sparked accusations of rights violations, appears prepared for more than just finding the four lost soldiers.
On 10 November, he boasted of having destroyed the "headquarters" of one of Haiti's main gangs, accompanied by video footage of the helicopter attack.
Since then, Bukele's forces have taken over a football stadium in the capital with the support of Haiti's national police.
On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called on all security forces to protect the population and resort to lethal force only as a last resort.
In the first 10 months of 2026, the UN recorded 4,595 deaths and 2,050 injuries to armed violence in Haiti.
In Miami over the weekend, at a football match between Haiti and the United States, some Haitian fans cheered on both their national team and Bukele, expressing high hopes the island's gangs can be contained.
Despite the 6-0 loss to the US in the Concacaf Nations League match, Haitians expressed optimism, waving Salvadoran flags and shouting "Bukele! Bukele!"
"All I can say is 'Viva Bukele!'," said 41-year-old Haitian fan Guito Ledix, adding that Bukele "is the only one trying to see if there's any possibility of getting rid of the gangs."
Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has faced a deep political and security crisis for years, with gangs seizing control of the island nation through a campaign of violence marked by murder, kidnapping and rape.
From Miami, home to one of the largest concentrations of Haitian immigrants, 28-year-old Stephanie Jeanty frets about the safety of her family still living there.
"Before I was a bit more stressed, but now, seeing the Salvadoran delegation that is working to restore peace, it's something, things are better," she said.
"I would really like to go back to my country. For now, no."

Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy
Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts.
As households brace for the colder winter months with household gas and electricity costs soaring, the latest figures push the headline inflation rate to the highest level in a year.
Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate.
“Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices respectively.”
Fuel prices for motorists rose at an annual rate of 33.2%, the largest increase since July 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sparked a global increase in energy prices.
The average price of petrol rose by 5.2.p a litre between September and October to reach 174.7p a litre, the highest level in four years. Diesel prices rose by 7p a litre to 199.5p a litre, the highest price on records dating back to 1996.
Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.
At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20 million households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.
However, a new forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight on Wednesday predicted a 26% jump in energy bills in Great Britain from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.
Forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.
Earlier this month Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.
Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year. Analysts said the Bank could be forced to raise borrowing costs from as early as next month.
Core inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – was unchanged at 2.8%, matching economists’ forecasts. Services inflation, which the Bank has been monitoring closely for evidence of domestic inflationary pressures becoming entrenched, also held steady at 3.7%, slightly below City predictions for a rate of 3.8%.
Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October amid an increase in long-haul ticket prices – offset by a downward effect from European flights. Prices for alcohol and tobacco also rose, by 4.5%, influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty at the start of the month.
Food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September.
The latest figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October. Driven by rising wholesale gas prices, forecasters are warning of a further increase of as much as a quarter from January.
However, wholesale energy prices have fallen back since the blow to Donald Trump’s authority after the US midterm elections, amid hopes for a negotiated breakthrough in the Middle East conflict.
Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world.
“The household energy payment, announced in our budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January, which will help to give families breathing space now.
“The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art:
Senegal were stripped of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title by a Confederation of African Football appeals board, and are awaiting the outcome of their own appeal at the Court of Arbitration for Sport
Senegal became the first side to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations before Cameroon and Morocco were among five others to join them with two games to spare - but there was penalty drama in Tripoli.
Tunisia, who have appeared at a record 17 consecutive editions of Afcon, are at risk of missing out after a contentious 1-1 draw against Libya.
Libya's penalty equaliser just before half-time followed protest scenes lasting over five minutes as players and staff from the Carthage Eagles challenged the decision.
The video assistant referee system is not used in Afcon qualifying, and Tunisia's remonstrating with the fourth official on the touchline ultimately only served to delay the spot-kick, which Ezoo El Mariamy, the player who was adjudged to have been fouled, converted.
Drawing the game meant Tunisia's winless start in Group H continued, with the Carthage Eagles having just three points from four games.
Tunisia need a strong finish to their campaign to give themselves a chance of reaching the finals, and Nigeria are also at risk of missing out, but others have made short order of qualifying.
Led by new head coach Patrick Vieira, Senegal moved to the brink of a place at the finals by beating Sudan 4-2 on Monday, and the Teranga Lions had their passage from Group J confirmed on Tuesday when Mozambique secured a 1-0 victory away against Ethiopia.
Cameroon and Benin also progressed without kicking a ball after Comoros and Burkina Faso registered wins - with the latter result also sealing a finals spot for the victorious Stallions.
Mali and Morocco extended their perfect starts and booked their places with triumphs over Rwanda and Niger respectively.
Abdellah Ouazane was the match-winner for Morocco in an away game that was actually played in Rabat, with the 17-year-old brilliantly curling in midway through the first half to cap a fine team move.
The Atlas Lions and Senegal are still waiting for the outcome of a case at the Court of Arbitration for Sport to decide the destination of the 2025 Afcon title.
Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time but Morocco were awarded the trophy by a Confederation of African Football appeals board which decreed the West Africans breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.
Cameroon, Senegal and Benin close in on Afcon 2027 qualification
Eleven sides had the chance to join co-hosts Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda at next year's finals when the fourth round of fixtures culminated on Tuesday.
Algeria, DR Congo, Egypt and the Ivorians all could have qualified with away wins but failed to pick up three points.
Brighton forward Yankuba Minteh was on target as The Gambia came from behind to lead Ivory Coast 2-1 in Group C, but Christ Inao Oulai grabbed an equaliser deep in stoppage time after Scorpions striker Muhammed Badamosi was sent off in the 90th minute.
Egypt were held to a goalless draw in Malawi, Sierra Leone claimed a late point against the Congolese and Algeria suffered a 3-0 defeat in Togo.
Angola beat South Sudan 1-0 in Juba and would have qualified had Egypt claimed victory in the other match in Group B.
Nigeria are in danger of failing to reach Afcon for the first time since 2017 after the Super Eagles failed to beat Tanzania.
The final two rounds of qualifiers will be held in March next year, with Afcon 2027 scheduled to be held in East Africa from 19 June to 17 July.
Malawi goalkeeper George Chikooka helped deny Mohamed Salah's Egypt an early passage to the Afcon 2027 finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda
Seven-time Afcon winners Egypt knew victory in Lilongwe could take them to the finals but were frustrated by an inspired second-half showing from Malawi goalkeeper George Chikooka.
After Pharaohs captain Mohamed Salah had hit the outside of the post from a tight angle, Chikooka denied Trezeguet and Haissem Hassan before also making fine stops from Mohamed Hany and Ibrahim Adel in stoppage time.
Egypt move on to eight points in Group B, two points behind Angola after Miro's first-half effort secured a 1-0 victory for the Palancas Negras in Juba.
There was drama as Ivory Coast salvaged a draw in Bakau through Inao Oulai's 98th-minute goal, which denied The Gambia a third win in Group C.
The Ivorians lead the pool on 10 points, with The Gambia on seven and Ghana on six following the Black Stars' back-to-back wins over Somalia.
DR Congo appeared on track to progress from Group E as Junior Kadile gave the Leopards a half-time lead in their away tie against Sierra Leone, but Alie Conteh netted in the 94th minute for the West Africans.
And Togo moved a point behind Group I leaders Algeria after a strong first-half showing in Lome, with two goals from Thibault Klidje before Kennedy Boateng's powerful header secured a 3-0 win over the 2019 champions from North Africa.

With East Africans Tanzania already assured of a spot at the finals, as co-hosts, Nigeria are competing with Guinea-Bissau for just one qualification spot available in Group L.
And Guinea-Bissau established a three-point advantage over the Super Eagles as goals from Mama Balde and Mauro Rodrigues gave them a 2-0 home win over Madagascar.

Tunisia's players and officials vehemently protested against the decision to award a foul after El Mariamy tussled with defender Ghaith Zaalouni and collided with goalkeeper Aymen Dahmen, delaying the penalty for several minutes.
The Tunisian visitors then had their own claims for a spot-kick turned down after a similar coming together between Mohamed Belhadj Mahmoud and Libya keeper Ayman Al Tihar, with players surrounding Beninois referee Adissa Ligali and his assistants at the full-time whistle.
The Carthage Eagles had also complained about refereeing decisions in the reverse fixture on Friday with a potential equaliser ruled out following a marginal offside call, before their North African neighbours sealed a 2-0 win.
Libya are one point behind Group H leaders Uganda after the Cranes drew 1-1 away against Botswana , who are one point better off than Tunisia.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are holding talks in Shenzhen, a day before a one-of-its-kind trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump in the southern Chinese city.
Chinese and Russian news agencies reported that the two leaders began talks around midday on Wednesday.
It was their fifth meeting this year, one of which took place by video link.
Thursday’s meeting has raised concern in Kyiv and European capitals that the three leaders could settle Ukraine’s future without them and divide the world into modern spheres of influence.
Washington initially said Ukraine was not expected to be on the agenda, but Trump later said it would be. Xi regards the war as not China’s concern.
Beijing has said only that the leaders will hold “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations” on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting.
According to Washington, the Iran war and nuclear disarmament are also on the table after the US-Russia bilateral nuclear weapons treaty expired in February. China has long argued that the US and Russia should cut their much larger arsenals before it will discuss limits on its own.
Opening the event, Xi called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence and free trade. China would pursue “deep-seated reform”, he said, starting with lower tariffs, wider market access and work on regulation and management standards.
Putin, who has been shunned by the West since he invaded Ukraine in 2022, told the APEC gathering he expected the trilateral to be “highly useful”.
With military and political risks rising, he said, “what is desperately needed is unity rather than division... and dialogue rather than ultimatums.”
He also argued that Western sanctions had failed, saying they could not fully halt growth or wreck the economies of rival states.
Trump was still in the Philippines on Wednesday, where he attended a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). A day earlier he met fellow Quad leaders from Australia, Japan and India for the first time in his second term. The group is broadly seen as a counterweight to Chinese influence in the region.
He said he hoped to hold one-on-one talks with both Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Shenzhen, adding that Kim “would like” to meet in China.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Manila, stopped short of confirming a Kim meeting but said engagement was the only way to resolve problems with North Korea.
Around 2,000 people protested during Trump’s visit, carrying banners reading “Trump out now” and “Reject Pax Silica”, a reference to a US supply chain initiative.

Northern Ireland are in the Nations League top-flight after topping their group after a draw in Hungary; Barnabas Varga ended Northern Ireland's proud record of not having conceded in this campaign but Justin Devenny equalised
Justin Devenny's superb strike saw Northern Ireland earn promotion to the top tier of the Nations League with a hard-fought 1-1 draw away to closest challengers Hungary in Budapest.
Barnabas Varga ended Northern Ireland's proud record of not having conceded in this campaign when he fired the hosts in front after 35 minutes - a goal that also sent Hungary to the top of the group.
But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for Michael O'Neill's young side, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland's one-point advantage as group leaders.
The visitors were on the back foot for much of the first half, with Hungary captain Dominik Szoboszlai hitting the post, but O'Neill, serving a touchline ban in the stands as former captain Steven Davis led things from the touchline, orchestrated key substitutions.
Northern Ireland started with Patrick Kelly in place of the suspended Jamie Donley up front but brought on Josh Magennis at half-time before Kieran Morrison and Brodie Spencer soon followed to help the visitors become a much greater threat going forward.
Magennis' physical presence and the extra pace paid dividends as, just two years after earning promotion from League C, Northern Ireland completed an unbeaten campaign in Group B2 to secure their place at the top table of European football.
Without Donley, the lack of a clear outlet told in a first half that saw Hungary come forward time and again.
There was a big panic after five minutes following an uncharacteristic mistake from Pierce Charles, whose pass went straight to Bendeguez Bolla, a late change to the Hungary side, who whipped in a superb low cross from which skipper Szoboszlai struck the post.
Northern Ireland were pegged back but might have snatched the lead from a Ciaron Brown long throw in the 33rd minute. However, Tom Atcheson did not seem to realise how much space he had as he prodded a weak shot towards his Blackburn team-mate Balazs Toth.
Two minutes later Pierce Charles launched a long free-kick into the box. Brown went down under an Andras Schafer challenge, but as Northern Ireland appealed in vain for a penalty, Toth kicked it long. Trai Hume got his head to the ball but could not get it as far as Pierce Charles, allowing Varga to nip in and score.
O'Neill will have felt the frustration of his ban with his side trailing at half-time, but his changes worked regardless.
Terry Devlin, the matchwinner on Saturday, had already fired into the side-netting before Price's low strike from the edge of the box cannoned back off the post.
Four minutes later they were level. Hume's long throw almost fell for Shea Charles but instead sat up for Devenny to take a touch before thumping an unstoppable strike into the top corner.
As time ticked down, Hungary pushed forward in increasing desperation - with Rajmund Toth firing over late on - but Northern Ireland dug in with the defensive resilience which has been the cornerstone of this campaign.
Northern Ireland boss Michael O'Neill speaking at his post-match press conference:
"It's a great feeling for us. We set out when we came into this level of the competition to first of all try and stay and we knew to be in the top two positions would help us.
"We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028 (qualification), but to come away unbeaten, to finish top, and to give the performance we've given against some very good teams, it's very encouraging.
"We had to dig really deep. We had to make substitutions; we had to try and get freshness. I felt in the first half we looked a little bit leggy, which is natural, but I just felt we needed that freshness at the right points in the game.
"But it was the belief we could get back into the game. We did that, and it was the belief that we could see the game out."
On Deveny's equaliser: "I was surrounded by Hungarian supporters, so I had to be slightly restrained! It was a celebration which was muted, shall we say!"

Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death
A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.
Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
Suleimani, the head of Iran’s foreign military operations, was killed in a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. Iranian officials have repeatedly vowed to avenge his killing.
Merchant had testified that he was forced into the plot to protect his family in the Iranian capital Tehran from the Guards, adding that he thought he would get caught before anyone was killed, multiple media outlets reported.
He said he was never ordered to kill a specific person but noted his Iranian contact had mentioned three people in connection with the plot – Trump, the former US president Joe Biden and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley.
But the United States attorney general, Todd Blanche, insisted on Tuesday that the plot was against Donald Trump.
“An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” said Blanche after Merchant was sentenced to 330 months’ imprisonment.
“The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.”
US officials previously said Merchant had “close ties to Iran” and described his alleged plot as “straight out of the Iranian regime’s playbook”.
Merchant was arrested on 12 July 2024 as he planned to leave the country.

Daithi O’Corrain, 48, has been charged with damaging a US military C-130 aircraft while it was parked overnight.
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”.
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians .
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property.
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.
According to prosecutors, he then breached security at Shannon Airport on April 11 and barricaded himself inside the parked aircraft.
He allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines and smashed every gauge in the cockpit.
O’Corrain also inflicted damage on the exterior of the aircraft with an axe, prosecutors said, and poured ball bearings into the transport plane’s fuel tanks.
“As a result of O’Corrain’s attack, the aircraft was effectively destroyed,” the office of the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York said in a statement.
“The damage inflicted rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the aircraft – worth approximately $60 million – will not return to active flight status.”
Shannon Airport, which was used by US President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a US military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a US military jet was parked.

Özel hayatını gizli tutmayı tercih eden Bilgin'in bu temkinli tutumu, hayatına İrem Uslu'nun girişinde de kendini göstermişti.

Antalya Emniyet Müdürlüğü ekipleri, zirvenin düzenlendiği Yeşil ve Mavi Bölge'de güvenlik önlemlerini sürdürüyor. Çevreci özellikleriyle öne çıkan polis timleri de ziyaretçilerin ilgisini çekiyor.
Çevik Kuvvet Şube Müdürlüğü bünyesindeki Atlı Polis Grup Amirliği ekipleri, Yeşil Bölge'de devriye görevi yapıyor.
Giriş ve çıkış kapıları ile kalabalığın yoğun olduğu etkinlik alanlarında devriye gezen atlı polisler, yerli ve yabancı katılımcılar tarafından ilgiyle karşılanıyor. Katılımcılarla fotoğraf da çektiren polisler, ziyaretçilerin sorularını yanıtlıyor.
Bölgede atlı polislerin yanı sıra eğitmenleri eşliğinde asayiş devriye köpekleri, elektrikli bagilerle görev yapan ekipler ve bisikletli polis timleri de güvenliği sağlıyor.
Zirvenin güvenliği kapsamında patlayıcı arama uzmanları, dedektör köpekler ile kimyasal, biyolojik, radyolojik ve nükleer keşif ekipleri de görev aldı.
Ekipler, zirve öncesinde ve organizasyon süresince yaklaşık 50 bin araç ile 50 otelde arama ve kontrol faaliyeti yürüttü.
Uluslararası organizasyonun güvenliğinin sağlanması için görev yapan ekipler, çalışmalarını titizlikle sürdürüyor.
Antalya Emniyet Müdürlüğü Çevik Kuvvet Şube Müdürlüğü Atlı Polis Grup Amirliğinde görevli komiser Abdurrahim Berk İncekara, AA muhabirine, COP31'de görev yapmaktan mutluluk duyduklarını söyledi.

Yerli ve yabancı katılımcıların büyük ilgisiyle karşılaşıyoruz. Gün boyu fotoğraf çekiyorlar. Atlar ve köpeklerle ilgili sorular soruyorlar. Tek tek hepsini bilgilendiriyoruz. Türkiye'nin ev sahipliğinde Antalya'da düzenlenen Birleşmiş Milletler (BM) İklim Değişikliği Çerçeve Sözleşmesi 31. Taraflar Konferansı'nın (COP31) operasyonel hazırlıkları, konaklamadan ulaşıma, konferans hizmetlerinden sıfır atık yönetimine kadar 31 ayrı iş başlığında yürütüldü.
Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanlığı Personel Genel Müdürü ve COP31 Operasyon Yönetimi Koordinatörü Halil Erdoğan, AA muhabirine, zirvenin hazırlık sürecini, organizasyonun operasyonel boyutunu ve alanın mimari tasarımında verilen kültürel mesajları anlattı.
Türkiye'nin COP31'e ev sahipliği yapacağının kesinleşmesinin ardından Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanı Murat Kurum'un talimatlarıyla çalışmalara başladıklarını belirten Erdoğan, günlük 100 bin, toplamda ise 1,5 milyon ziyaretçi öngörüsüyle hazırlık yaptıklarını söyledi.
Erdoğan, konaklama, lojistik, güvenlik, sağlık, ulaşım, konferans hizmetleri, tercüme, medya ve yayın, temizlik ve sıfır atık yönetimi dahil 31 ayrı başlıkta operasyonu planladıklarını ifade etti.

Erdoğan, organizasyonun ardından da kullanılabilecek kalıcı yapılar oluşturmayı hedeflediklerini, böylece EXPO alanını yeniden Antalya'ya kazandırdıklarını dile getirdi.
Önceki COP zirvelerinde numaralarla anılan konferans salonlarına Türkiye'nin doğal ve kültürel mirasını yansıtan isimler verdiklerini ifade eden Erdoğan, ana salona "Anadolu", diğer salonlara ise Akdeniz, Ayder, Kaçkar, Van Gölü ve Göbeklitepe gibi isimler koyduklarını aktardı.
Erdoğan, basın merkezlerine de Mevlana ve Yunus Emre isimlerini vererek dünyanın farklı ülkelerinden gelen gazetecilere sevgi, hoşgörü ve dayanışma mesajı vermeyi amaçladıklarını belirtti.

İstanbul Aile Mahkemesi ’ne sunulan dava dilekçesinde, şu ifadelere yer verildi: “Gökhan Töre, eve alkollü şekilde zorla girerek çalışanları tehdit etmiş ve eşine ait değerli tüm tabloları almıştır. Müvekkil, hemen eşiyle ortak kasasının olduğu bankaya gitmiş, kasayı kontrol ettiğinde Gökhan Töre tarafından boşaltıldığını öğrenmiştir. Evli oldukları dönemde tüm malvarlığı baskıyla Gökhan Töre üzerine kaydedilmiştir.”
HIRS ve öfkeyle hareket eden Gökhan Töre ’nin, tüm malvarlığını yok edeceğini ve üçüncü kişilere devredeceğini ifade ettiği belirtilen dilekçede, “Özellikle Muğla’daki 4 taşınmaz üzerinde müvekkilin çok büyük emeği vardır. Bu sebeple Gökhan Töre adına kayıtlı Muğla’daki 4 taşınmaz ile satılığa çıkardığı 3 adet değerli araç olmak üzere tüm araçların üçüncü kişilere devrinin önlenmesi için mahkemeden tedbir kararı verilmesini talep ediyoruz” denildi.
Türkiye ve dünyadaki en güncel gelişmelerden haberdar olmak için, bültenlerin gönderileceği e-posta adresini girin.
